title: Right and Wrong
theme: Ethics: duty, conscience and moral choice
objectives: I can use ethics, moral, virtue, and conscience to discuss what makes an action right or wrong.
I can tell accountable, culpable, and complicit apart by asking who did what and who is responsible.
I can explain why an action might be altruistic and why motives can still be mixed.
I can use the word parts -al, -ic, and -able to build and read describing words.
rationale: Ethical reasoning needs abstract words that students can argue with, and grade 8 is the first year when literature, history, and civics all ask 'what should this person have done?' The ten words fall into three groups: the ideas themselves (ethics, ethical, moral, virtue, conscience), the question of who is responsible (accountable, culpable, complicit), and how people respond to wrongdoing or to need (altruistic, atone). Accountable, culpable, and complicit are taught as a set because students blur them. The passage places them in a situation close to students' lives, an online group, so that the words carry weight without being tied to a famous historical case. Students will use these words in character analysis, historical judgment, and argument writing.

words.def: The study of right and wrong, and the beliefs about good conduct that a person or group lives by.
words.ex: The school's ethics club debates questions such as whether it is fair to keep a secret that could protect someone.
words.ex2: A journalist's code of ethics requires her to correct any mistake that she makes in print.
words.nonExample: A list of the cafeteria's lunch prices has nothing to do with ethics.

apps.academic: In social studies, ethics asks whether a leader's choices were right, not just whether they worked.
apps.spoken: It's a question of ethics, not only rules.
apps.writing: Use ethics for the system of beliefs behind a decision; use ethical for a choice that fits those beliefs.

words.def: Required to explain or accept responsibility for your actions and their results.
words.ex: Student leaders are accountable to the class for how they spend the club's money.
words.ex2: The coach held himself accountable for the loss instead of blaming the referees.

apps.academic: Citizens hold leaders accountable by asking them to explain their decisions in public.
apps.spoken: I'm accountable for my own choices.

words.def: An inner sense of right and wrong that guides your actions and makes you feel guilty when you do wrong.

words.ex2: She had a clear conscience because she had told the truth.

words.def: Caring about the well-being of others and acting to help them without expecting a reward.

words.ex2: Some animals show altruistic behavior, such as warning the group of danger at a risk to themselves.

apps.academic: Ethicists ask whether a truly altruistic act exists if the helper also feels good afterward.
apps.spoken: It was kind of her, and honestly pretty altruistic.

cloze2.s: Her ___ act was giving away her last concert ticket to a stranger who had traveled far, expecting nothing in return.

words.frame: An altruistic act is one that ___ without expecting ___.

words.def: Involved in a wrongdoing along with others, even without taking the leading role.
words.ex: The bystanders who cheered the prank became complicit in it.
words.ex2: A company that knows about a hidden danger and says nothing may be complicit in the harm that follows.
words.nonExample: A person who reports a wrongdoing right away is not complicit in it.

apps.academic: Historians ask whether ordinary people who stayed silent were complicit in the actions of their government.
apps.spoken: If you laugh along, you're a little bit complicit.
apps.writing: Use complicit for someone who shares in a wrong by helping, hiding, or staying silent.

cloze.s: Although she never touched the paint, Rina felt ___ because she had kept watch while her friends sprayed the wall.

cloze2.s: The mayor was ___ in the cover-up, since he knew about the broken pump and signed papers to hide it.

misuse.s: The student who reported the cheating at once was complicit in the cheating.
misuse.why: Reporting a wrong immediately is the opposite of sharing in it.

visual.alt: Several people exchanging a secret look.

words.def: Deserving blame for something wrong that you did or allowed to happen.
words.ex: The driver was found culpable for the crash because she had been texting at the time.
words.ex2: Are the students who only watched the prank as culpable as the ones who planned it?
words.nonExample: A person who was far away when something happened is not culpable for it.

apps.academic: Courts and historians both ask how culpable each person was, not only whether something went wrong.
apps.spoken: I'm culpable for part of this, so I'll help fix it.
apps.writing: Use culpable for blame that is earned; it is more formal than guilty and often asks how much blame.

cloze.s: The report found the company ___ for the spill because it had ignored three warnings about the leaking tank.

cloze2.s: A child who breaks a window by accident is less ___ than one who throws a rock at it on purpose.

misuse.s: The jury found the defendant culpable, so the judge announced that he had no responsibility for the harm.
misuse.why: Culpable means deserving blame; having no responsibility is the opposite.

visual.alt: A pointing finger beside a balance scale.

words.def: To make up for a wrong you have done by apologizing or by acting to repair the harm.
words.ex: He tried to atone for breaking the window by paying for the repair and writing an apology.
words.ex2: In the story, the sailor spends the rest of his life trying to atone for abandoning his crew.
words.nonExample: Saying "sorry" and then repeating the same harmful act does not atone for anything.

apps.academic: Many stories follow a character who must atone for a mistake before the conflict can be resolved.
apps.spoken: How can I atone for forgetting your birthday?
apps.writing: Use atone for actions that repair harm, not just for words of regret.

cloze.s: To ___ for forgetting her friend's birthday, she planned a surprise dinner and apologized sincerely.

cloze2.s: Years later, the company tried to ___ for polluting the river by paying for a full cleanup.

misuse.s: She atoned for the mistake by blaming someone else and pretending that nothing had happened.
misuse.why: To atone is to make up for a wrong; blaming someone else makes it worse.

passage.title: Who Is Responsible?
paras: In Mr. Alder's ethics elective, the question on the board was blunt: "Who is responsible when a group does something wrong?" Nobody answered at first. Dani stared at her desk. The week before, she had watched a group chat fill up with an edited photo of a boy named Teo, and she had said nothing.

Cole had made the photo, and he was plainly accountable for it, since he had changed the picture and posted it. Mr. Alder wanted the class to think about everyone else. "Were the students who laughed culpable?" he asked. "They did not make the photo. Are they guilty of anything?" Mia answered, "Not by law, maybe. But it might still be a moral problem."

Mr. Alder explained that ethics is the study of how people should act. "An ethical choice does not only avoid punishment," he said. "It asks what a person of good character would do. Courage and honesty are examples of a virtue, and some philosophers say we build a virtue by practicing it." Then he asked, "If I watch a wrong and say nothing, am I complicit?"

Dani raised her hand slowly. "I did not make it," she said, "but I laughed. My conscience has bothered me for a week." The room went quiet. Mr. Alder nodded. "That discomfort is useful," he said. "It means something inside you is paying attention."

Dani decided to atone. She wrote Teo a note without excuses, and she deleted the photo from every device she controlled. She also asked the principal to start a peer group about kindness online. Her friend Raj called the idea altruistic, but Dani shook her head. "It is not only for Teo," she admitted. "It is partly for me." Mr. Alder smiled. "Motives are rarely pure," he said. "The ethical question is whether anyone was helped."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Mr. Alder asks whether the students who laughed were "culpable." He is asking whether they
choices: were able to laugh quietly
deserve some of the blame
can prove they were innocent
were punished by the school
qs.why: Culpable means deserving blame, and he follows the word with the question "Are they guilty of anything?"

qs.q: Why does Mr. Alder call Dani's discomfort "useful"?
choices: It will help her avoid detention.
It shows her conscience is working and can guide her next step.
It proves that she was the one who made the photo.
It means she should keep her thoughts to herself.
qs.why: He says it means something inside her is paying attention, which describes a working conscience.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Cole is accountable for the photo?
choices: He changed the picture and then posted it.
He sat near Dani in the elective.
He laughed with the other students.
He was not mentioned in Mr. Alder's lesson.
qs.why: Cole made and posted the photo, so he is the one who must answer for it.

qs.q: Why does Dani say that her plan is "partly for me"?
choices: She wants to be named in the principal's report.
She believes Teo will never read her note.
She hopes that her own guilt will feel lighter if she helps.
She does not think the plan will help anyone.
qs.why: Dani admits that the plan is not purely for Teo, and she has already said that her conscience has bothered her for a week.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: People are responsible only for what they do alone.
A joke is never harmful when many people share it.
Responsibility can extend beyond the person who caused harm, and making amends involves action.
A conscience is something only adults have.
qs.why: The passage separates the one who made the photo from the others who laughed and then shows Dani taking action to repair the harm.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for reasoning about right and wrong, read a short narrative about responsibility in an online group chat, practice the endings -al, -ic, and -able, and write about a moral choice. The unit's habit is to name who did what, how much they are responsible, and what could repair the harm.

notes.va.ethics.n: Ethics is the study of right and wrong and the beliefs behind choices. Students may think ethics means rules; point out that a rule can be unethical. Ask for an example of a legal action that some people consider unethical. Use school-appropriate examples and avoid divisive current events.
notes.va.ethical.adj: Ethical is the adjective. It describes choices, not people (a person is 'ethical' or 'has ethics', but the stronger use is for the choice). Model the base ethic + -al. Practice by judging three short scenarios and defending each verdict.
notes.va.moral.adj: Moral is both an adjective (a moral question) and a noun (the moral of the story). Teach the adjective and show the noun on the word card. Students may use moral and ethical interchangeably; both are fine here, but point out that ethical often refers to a professional or formal code.
notes.va.accountable.adj: Accountable is answerable: someone must explain and accept the result. It includes the question, 'accountable to whom?' Use leaders and club treasurers. Contrast with blame: a leader can be accountable even if she was not at fault.
notes.va.conscience.n: Conscience is the inner sense that judges your own actions, a bit like an inner voice. Students sometimes confuse it with consciousness; the words are related but different. Use a literary example of guilt and a clear conscience. Treat the topic gently and avoid asking for personal confessions.
notes.va.virtue.n: Virtue is a good quality of character. Offer a list (honesty, courage, patience, fairness) and have students pick one and show it with a small action. Note the difference between a virtue and a talent. The word has a second everyday sense in 'by virtue of'; do not teach it here.
notes.va.altruistic.adj: Altruistic means helping without expecting a reward. Discuss whether pure altruism exists; the passage shows mixed motives. Model altruist + -ic. Do not let the discussion shame students for feeling good about helping; the point is to examine motives, not to condemn them.
notes.va.complicit.adj: Complicit means sharing in a wrong. A person can be complicit by helping, hiding, or staying silent. Keep examples close to school life. Ask 'What could she have done instead?' so the discussion moves toward action rather than blame alone.
notes.va.culpable.adj: Culpable means deserving blame. It is more formal than guilty, and it invites degrees: more culpable, less culpable. Contrast with accountable. Use a sequence of scenarios (accident, carelessness, deliberate act) to show a scale of culpability.
notes.va.atone.v: Atone means making up for a wrong through action. Stress that words alone are not enough. Some students find it helpful to remember that the word is sometimes explained as 'at one,' meaning to be at peace again; share this as a memory aid only. Pair with apologize and repair.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Cole made the photo, so he is accountable. The students who laughed did not make it, but they shared in it, so they might be complicit. Whether they are culpable depends on how much blame they deserve. Dani's conscience is bothering her, which tells me she believes she did something wrong, and her plan to atone shows her taking action.'
discuss: What makes an apology count as atoning rather than only saying sorry?
How should a group decide how much blame each member deserves?
misconceptions: Ethics and law are the same thing.
A person is culpable only if they did the act themselves.
Altruistic means weak or too nice.
A good conscience means never making mistakes.
extend: Write a short scene in which a character's conscience changes a decision, and underline the unit words.
Choose a historical or literary figure and write a paragraph arguing whether the person was accountable, complicit, or culpable.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to accountable/culpable/complicit as a set after two days with a new scenario, and at one week in a short written verdict. The earlier words skew and omit return when students judge how an account of a wrongdoing might have been distorted, and benevolent returns as a way to describe a motive.

wida.oral: Partner A describes a short scenario about a group doing something wrong. Partner B says who is accountable, who is complicit, and who is not, and explains with one word from the unit.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: ética, ético, moral, responsable (accountable; the English and Spanish words differ in how much they stress answering to others), conciencia (also means awareness), virtud, altruista, cómplice, culpable, expiar (atone; formal).
Cognate flags for ética, ético, moral, conciencia, virtud, altruista, cómplice, and culpable should be confirmed.

Etymology: atone is described only as a memory aid ('at one') in the teacher note; no etymology claim appears in student-facing fields. No morph is given for conscience, virtue, complicit, culpable, or atone.
Sense boundary: moral is taught as an adjective with the noun sense (the moral of a story) shown as a second sense.
